title: How the Secret Service Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the U.S. Secret Service: its origins in 1865 as a counterfeiting-fighting agency (signed by Lincoln the day he was killed), its later expansion to presidential protection after McKinley's assassination in 1901, its non-protection duties (fraud, cybercrime through Electronic Crimes Task Forces, the ink and handwriting libraries), staffing and morale problems, the Presidential Protection Division and its demanding shift schedules, advance work and site security, budget strain, hiring requirements and training, the Reagan assassination attempt and agent Jerry Parr's response, the JFK assassination and agents' partying, recent scandals (Cartagena, Amsterdam, the 2014 White House shooting and intrusion), and a few trivia items. The episode closes with a listener mail about the Satanic Temple's core tenets.

segments.title: Opening banter and overview
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Secret Service, noting its protection role is secondary in staffing to its original law enforcement duties, and discuss the agency's staffing and the first non-agent director.

segments.title: Origins and early presidential protection
segments.summary: Lincoln signed the legislation creating the Secret Service in 1865 the day he was killed, mainly to fight counterfeiting. Protection of presidents came later, after the Cleveland plot and McKinley's 1901 assassination, when three agents were nearby.

segments.title: Staffing, morale and workplace culture
segments.summary: The agency is understaffed and overworked, with low morale; a 2016 federal survey ranked it last of 305 agencies for employee satisfaction. Hiring has added staff since, partly due to the current president's large family.

segments.title: Expanded duties and protected persons
segments.summary: Beyond the president and vice president, the agency protects families, former presidents, candidates, and visiting dignitaries as needed, while State Department security covers foreign heads of state. Other responsibilities include National Special Security Events and absorbed agencies such as the Treasury Police and White House Police.

segments.title: Electronic Crimes Task Forces
segments.summary: Electronic Crimes Task Forces were created after 9/11 and the Patriot Act to fight cybercrime, including data breaches, network intrusions, forensics, identity theft, and credit card theft.

segments.title: Presidential Protection Division and advance work
segments.summary: The Presidential Protection Division is the most visible unit. Hosts discuss Clinton and Reagan's jogging and horseback riding, the demanding rotating shift schedule, the myth of an oath to take a bullet, and advance work such as site sweeps, escape routes, and employee background checks at hotels and restaurants.

segments.title: Standing posts, video unit and food security
segments.summary: Agents perform standing post duty to guard stairwells, the video unit films motorcades, and Secret Service staff watch White House kitchen food. Presidential pizza orders are sent to the Naval Observatory.

segments.title: Budget strain and the Trump Tower trailer
segments.summary: The agency's protective operations cost about $750 million annually, roughly half its budget, and it reportedly ran short of funds. A dispute over office space at Trump Tower led to a trailer on the sidewalk outside.

segments.title: Ink library, handwriting database and investigations
segments.summary: The agency keeps an ink library of thousands of inks and pens for comparing evidence, along with the forensic handwriting database known as FISH. It also assists with missing and exploited children and makes counterfeiting busts, such as a 2016 Lima, Peru seizure.

segments.title: Hiring, training and Reagan assassination attempt
segments.summary: Applicants must be 21 to 37, pass screening, a polygraph, and a background check, then complete training at Glynco, Georgia and the James J. Rowley Training Center. Training includes ten-minute medicine and blood on hand. The hosts recount the 1981 Reagan shooting by John Hinckley Jr. and agent Jerry Parr's response.

segments.title: JFK assassination, scandals, trivia and listener mail
segments.summary: Discussion of agents partying before the JFK assassination, the limo driver's response, and recent scandals in Colombia, El Salvador, and Amsterdam, and the 2014 White House shooting and fence-jumping intrusion. Trivia follows, then a listener mail about Satanic Temple tenets.
